items.body: The title of Emna Mâaref‘s first solo full-length comes from a verse by the tenth-century Arab poet Abu Firas al-Hamdani, roughly asking, “Has longing no hold over you?” Yet hawa encompasses love, desire, attraction and surrender, and Mâaref describes these impulses as the engine behind her creative life. Across Ama Lel Hawa, longing generates movement: through maqām, improvisation and an oud vocabulary shaped by two decades of playing alongside her experience with electronics, sound design and cinema. Recorded at Montreal’s Hotel2Tango in a single day, the pieces were improvised or partially composed within frameworks established beforehand. “الخطبة البتراء” opens ceremonially, while “Ouverture ’25” and “Improvisation I” progressively loosen that initial concentration, allowing phrases, resonance and silence to determine the music’s direction. Mâaref’s knowledge of maqām provides the underlying grammar, but the music remains sensuous and exploratory, constantly finding new routes through familiar materials. The album opens further when other musicians enter. On the title track, Lounis Adjissa’s bass gives the oud additional depth and physical weight, while “Afa2estas9aynakumuha” introduces Habib El Bardi’s saxophone and electronics, extending Mâaref’s melodic language into a more ambiguous acoustic space. Both appear on “Wa Na7ya”, where oud, saxophone, electronics and bass move around one another without settling into conventional accompaniment. These pieces also connect the album to Mâaref’s wider practice: oud, electronics and sound design emerge as different parts of the same musical vocabulary. “From Hadrumetum to Tiohtià:ke (And Back Insha2allah)” brings another kind of longing into view. Its journey from ancient Hadrumetum, present-day Sousse, to Tiohtià:ke/Montréal turns geographical distance into musical space, with the promised return left suspended in insha’Allah. The final improvisations bring Mâaref back to the oud alone, probing attacks, silences and decaying resonance. Ama Lel Hawa ultimately feels both deeply rooted and unsettled: tradition remains a living language through which Mâaref can articulate desire, displacement and change. Photo by Nick Jewell To find out more about the production process of Ama Lel Hawa we have reached out directly to Emna Mâaref. Ama Lel Hawa is introduced through Abu Firas al-Hamdani’s famous verses on longing, yet the album rarely feels nostalgic in a conventional sense. Instead, longing seems to function almost as a creative force that continually pushes the music forward. How did that poem become the conceptual centre of the album, and what does “hawa” mean to you beyond its imperfect English translations as “love” or “passion”? For me, love and passion are essential. I don’t think I could do what I do, make music, pursue artistic discipline, or even move through life, without them. They are the engine behind everything, the force that gives me motivation and keeps me moving forward. In that sense, hawa is much more than simply “love” or “passion.” It carries something more unstable and difficult to contain: desire, longing, attraction, attachment, perhaps even a kind of surrender to something that pulls you. My connection to Abu Firas al-Hamdani was not necessarily a particular fascination with him as a historical figure. It was more an attraction to this poem and, especially, to some of its verses. I have always been passionate about history, and many of the references in the album’s titles come from that interest. But I am also deeply drawn to Arabic poetry. I read it constantly, and I often find myself reciting or singing poems to my friends. At the beginning of the project, I had many different titles in mind for the album. After the recording session at Hotel2Tango, we went out to celebrate at a bar. At some point, I recited the entire verse, and “Ama Lel Hawa” came out almost spontaneously. Habib and Ghazi immediately said, “By the way, that’s an amazing title.” And that was it, we chose it. I love the poem, and I find it incredibly rich, but I think my decision to take the album’s title from it came more from my relationship with the Arabic language and Arabic poetry in general. So perhaps the title emerged quite naturally from that relationship, rather than from a preconceived conceptual decision. Ama Lel Hawa is deeply rooted in the tradition of the oud and the maqām system, yet you seem to approach the oud almost as a sound designer. Has your work with electronics changed the way you physically listen to and perform the instrument? Absolutely! Working with electronics has given me a broader perspective on sound in general. Whether you choose to play the instrument in a more traditional way or experiment with new techniques and sounds is ultimately a personal choice, or depends on the artistic vision of a particular project. But more generally, working with electronics has transformed the way I think about music. It has opened my practice to areas I didn’t know or explore before. Even though the oud and electronic music don’t necessarily share the same language or codes, as a player and an artist, the way you listen, think about, and design a sound or a musical project inevitably changes. It has definitely expanded and developed my perspective compared to before. Your recent soundtracks, particularly The Color of Phosphate and I’ve Known Rivers, are inseparable from landscape. Dust, desert, abandoned mining towns and geological spaces seem to shape the music as much as the images themselves. Ama Lel Hawa contains no environmental recordings, yet I often had the impression of listening to landscapes rather than solo performances. Do you think your experience composing for cinema has changed the way you imagine musical space, even when you’re recording the oud entirely on its own? Every experience we have teaches us something and helps us develop our practice. Cinema, for me, is one of the most inspiring art forms. Composing for film was one of my dreams, and I feel very lucky to have had the opportunity to realise it. I hope to continue developing this part and to have more opportunities to work in cinema. The films I have worked on, including The Color of Phosphate, I’ve Known Rivers, and another film, Barbary, which was selected for TIFF, as well as the sound work I have created for several art exhibitions, were all closely connected to the artistic vision of their directors and creators. When you compose or design sound for an image, you still have space to create freely, but the work itself and its creators also suggest certain directions and intentions. It’s interesting that Ama Lel Hawa can evoke a sense of landscape, even though the album contains no environmental recordings. I was trying to capture a particular phase in my life, connected to many emotions, especially distance and being far from my home country. Maybe this is what gives the music this feeling of openness or space. But for me, this project still has its own independent character and internal logic. The album was recorded in a single day, with pieces that were improvised or only partially composed, yet the performances never sound spontaneous in the casual sense. They feel architecturally coherent, as though years of musical knowledge are being distilled into a single gesture. How do you negotiate the balance between improvisation and the discipline of maqām, and at what point do you feel an improvisation has become a finished composition? The discipline of maqām is a large and fluid frame for improvisation. This is the first rule! What makes Oriental music so rich and interesting is that its sounds and melodies have to be sensuous. Obviously, there are theories, maqām trees, variations, patterns, and different schools of playing, but you have to feel it and find your own way of expressing yourself. I think this is the most important thing you have to learn. In this project, there are indeed a lot of improvised parts in certain tracks, but the general frame was already defined: the maqām, for example, and some transition phrases. It is improvisation within a predefined frame. During the preparation of the album, the rehearsals were dedicated to defining these frames. When I reached a certain feeling that this was how the album should be, we went to the studio and recorded the momentum itself. Because, to be honest, there is no finished composition in itself, you have to decide where it ends, or when it has reached a point of completion. For someone like me, if I don’t make that decision, it might take years before something is released—which was actually the case with many previous projects. Although Ama Lel Hawa is primarily a solo oud record, the three ensemble pieces with Habib El Bardi and Lounis Adjissa subtly transform the musical landscape without ever abandoning the album’s intimacy. What drew you to introduce those collaborations at those particular moments, and what possibilities emerge for the oud when it enters into dialogue with saxophone, electronics and bass rather than remaining entirely alone? Interacting with other musicians, as well as with electronic music, was always part of this project. From the beginning, the intention was to compose pieces involving other instruments. At some point, I was actually trying to do the opposite: to give the oud more space to exist on its own, because I initially wanted to add more instruments to other tracks as well. So the final result became what you hear on the album: a project where the oud is often alone, but where these other musical presences enter at particular moments. It wasn’t really about deciding that the oud should remain isolated, but rather about finding the right balance. For example, I’ve worked and performed live with Habib on several occasions, and we have an amazing ability to connect, exchange, and really enjoy what we’re doing together. His saxophone playing therefore felt very relevant to the project as a whole, and especially to the two tracks on which he appears. For the release concert, the instrumental parts will develop and extend further. I really love playing the oud with other instruments, and I feel that interaction and dialogue with other musicians inspire me a lot. Photo by Nick Jewell Your first electronic EP, Scars of Thorns, embraced heavy, abrasive textures inspired by hip-hop production and synthesis, while Ama Lel Hawa is almost entirely acoustic. On paper, they seem to belong to completely different musical worlds. Yet I wonder whether they are driven by the same curiosity about sound. Do you see these projects as separate identities, or are electronic production, film scoring and the oud simply different ways of asking the same musical questions? Not at all. Nothing is separate. Everything is happening inside my mind. It all comes from the same person, with this rich and varied lived experience. Every practice I engage in expresses different parts of me, frustrations, madness, love, tenderness. Nothing is isolated from the rest. Whether I am working with electronics, composing for film, or playing the oud, these are not separate identities or different musical worlds. They are simply different ways of expressing parts of the same person. Of course, certain sounds or musical approaches can express particular feelings more effectively than others. Sometimes something more sensitive or intimate calls for one kind of sound, while something more intense requires another. Sometimes you simply feel that you need a specific sound rather than another. This is what makes creating music with different tools so exciting: you have more possibilities and different ways of expressing what you want to express through music. But in terms of separate identities, I don’t see them as separate at all. (Gianmarco Del Re)

items.body: Last year, the Slovak band KIFOTH released their latest album, “Lost Territory”. In essence, it was more of an EP featuring four new tracks, followed by no fewer than nine remixes by other bands. This new album serves as a kind of addendum, revisiting those four tracks—along with an older song that originally appeared on their debut album, “Spectaclebreakers” (1999), and was also remixed on “Lost Territory”. What makes this release particularly interesting, however, is that the Slovak trio has taken on the task of remixing all the tracks themselves. In total, we get ten remixes, although some could almost be described as completely reworked and reinvented songs. That is not to say they sound radically different; KIFOTH remains, first and foremost, an EBM act—albeit one with a knack for intricate compositions and meticulous attention to detail. This is an intelligent form of EBM with a touch of FLA. The tracks are rich in sounds and effects, with icy tones propelled by powerful rhythms, while the deep, haunting vocals fit the atmosphere perfectly. Naturally, a record like this leaves room for experimentation, which perhaps explains the inclusion of certain orchestral arrangements. The same applies to several remixes featuring female vocals. While this is a new direction for KIFOTH, it creates a delightful contrast with their established sound. As far as I’m concerned, this is a highly successful experiment, as the album is certainly just as good as “Lost Territory”—if not better. (Rating:8). Listen to “Cowards – Dark Factory”: Cowards – Dark Factory by KIFOTH About KIFOTH KIFOTH formed in Slovakia in 1993 as Kneel In Front Of The Hangman, later renamed Kneel In Front Of The Executioner, built around K-head on music and mirColon on vocals. The duo played its first show in the summer of 1994 at the “Young Apollo” festival. KIFOTH self-released its debut album, “Spectaclebreakers,” in 1999, then moved to Out Of Line for two albums and to Vendetta Music for two more. “Violence Corporation” followed in 2010; a seven-year hiatus preceded “Extensive Report” on EK Product in 2017. Aliens Production announced “Artificial Territory” in June 2026, following the label’s “Lost Territory” release earlier that year.
items._cn_summary: 斯洛伐克三人组合KIFOTH的《Artificial Territory》是对其前作《Lost Territory》的延伸与变奏。专辑将原EP中的四首曲目连同一首来自1999年首张专辑的老歌重新混音，共产生十首作品，其中多首几乎等同于完全重塑。乐团保留EBM基底，却在制作中融入了管弦乐编排与女性人声采样，冰冷的音色与强劲节奏交织，深沉阴郁的人声贴合整体氛围。评论指出这种自我混音策略使制作细节更加精密，编排层次更为复杂，整体品质不逊于《Lost Territory》，某些层面甚至更优。对于偏好暗潮与工业电子的听众，这张专辑在保留类型辨识度的同时，以实验性的自我重制手法拓宽了声音边界。

items.body: What happens if the sun disappears? The question lingered over the stage at Viljandi Folk Festival on the morning of its closing day. Tell Your Birds brought it there, playing songs from a still unreleased record in front of a crowd for the first time. Kristīne Tukre‘s concert kokle carried the melodies, Vija Moore‘s percussion under them, Kärt Tambet‘s bowed hiiu kannel cut across both, and everything the three of them played ran through Simone Spampinato‘s processing. They sang in Estonian and Latvian at once, each keeping the language they grew up speaking. Some of the material comes from those same traditions, chopped up and rebuilt inside the band’s own songs. The rest belongs to no repertoire at all, written on the chance that one day it might. Straight after the set, in the last hour before Tell Your Birds broke apart for the rest of the summer, we sat down with the four of them not far from the stage, with a temperamental recorder giving us a hard time and cutting out every few minutes. Our chat eventually fell into the band’s own working rhythm: a burst, a stop, a burst. Tukre and Spampinato live in Helsinki, Tambet in Viljandi, Moore in Riga. They get a few days together, write everything in that stretch, then go back to their own cities until the next one. Today, as they release their new single, “Meneki Tükk”, we go back to that hour before they scattered, when they talked about where a tradition comes from and what you have to know before using it, about melodies written for a time that has not happened yet, and about the syllables that decide which language a song ends up in. Tell Your Birds started with a student project. All four met at the Sibelius Academy in Helsinki, in different departments, and Tambet dates the band from there: “We came together as a band back in 2023, but back then it was a very specific project. It was Vija [Moore], who is our percussionist, her bachelor concert project in Sibelius Academy in Finland, where we all studied together.” The concert took place in the same place where it was composed: in the Helsinki urban forest, yet recorded in forest near Ērgļi, a village in Latvia. They hauled the balafon, the percussion, the violin and the kokle out among the trees and played there, birds and insects carrying on around them and ending up on the tape along with everything else. For Spampinato that set the method for everything after it: “it was the first project where we all get together and thought, we recorded everything outside. We tried to record the instruments as they were part of the soundscape in that sense.” That turned into Pause in Nature, then Carry on with Hope, out on 1 November 2024. One year later they wanted more room to move, and Tambet marks autumn 2025 as the turn: “to write together and to think of music more widely, maybe not so specifically as we had done before“. Moore had been waiting for it: “I like that with this new music, we got to put it all together.” There was a lot to put together. The four met inside one institution and arrived there from four directions, and Moore starts with the two furthest from folk: “Simone comes from sound art, electronics, different sound design type of experience and worldview. And then Kristīne comes from a contemporary composition and contemporary kantele playing. Also, Kristīne is interested in baroque music.” She and Tambet are the two who came up in folk music, she through percussion, Tambet through singing and the violin. The spread is the point for Moore: “Each of us have a different genre outlook. I think it all comes together in our music, and it’s very interesting.“ Tukre’s own route ran through the classical kantele, though her instrument at home is the kokle. The Estonian kannel, the Latvian kokle and the Finnish kantele are cousins in one family of box zithers, and the family resemblance is where it gets interesting for her: “We have a very interesting phenomenon here in the Baltics and in Finland. We have these string instruments; they’re similar, but at the same time very different. They have different names, but we, musicians, try to come together.” The players of all three look across the borders to each other’s instruments. She did exactly that, a kokle player going to Helsinki to learn the kantele at the Sibelius Academy: “That’s how I got to Finland. I got to meet Vija, Kärt and Simone, and we started the band.“ Coming together now happens across three countries, which turns rehearsals and recording sessions into an exercise of dates, plans and travel tickets, so they work in blocks: several days in one of the three places, everything at once, then dispersal. For Moore the two halves stay separate: “We just intensively get into the music for those couple of days, and then go back to our real lives.” Where those blocks happen feeds the music too. “I also think us meeting for intensive times in different places has played a big role in the music. Because when we have come to Viljandi, we get to see into the Viljandi life, and we get to see into the whole Estonian culture, even social culture. It plays such a big role of explaining what a tradition means. And then also going to Latvia all together, that was the missing puzzle pieces.” Estonia, Latvia and Finland have all had their turn. Italy is still waiting, as Spampinato points out: “We have not been to Italy. What a terrible thing!” The residencies have gone further than rehearsal rooms and taken the four into each other’s family homes, which Moore counts as its own kind of source material: “In our residencies, it’s very nice that we’ve met each other’s families because families represent culture in a whole other coded way, it’s something not explainable by words.” What comes back from those weeks is a songbook the band builds itself. Tambet traces the bulk of it to the four of them: “Most of the music is actually original music that we have composed together, or separately, but brought it to this group.” Folk melodies feed into it, and so do myths, texts and lyrics that arrive as words alone. Before using any of it, Tambet wants the origin and the original purpose clear: “there’s a lot of using a tradition in music. But when doing so, you have to be aware of it, and be able to translate it to others. It’s highly important that we’re aware where the tradition is coming from and what the original intention behind that is, so we can put it into our own musical language.” The traditions Spampinato grew up with are not the ones on the table. He comes from Sicily, but his folk roots lie in Ciociaria, a historical region of southern Lazio: “My folk background is actually from Ciociaria, not Sicilian.” What he brings instead comes from sound art, electronics and sound design, where the tradition is the sound itself: “My background is more about sound. What do we do with every little sound?” Put that question to folk music and you get the music he admires most: “I’m really a huge fan of experimental French folk music, Sourdure for example, and I think we are trying to get into that.” In practice it means cutting material up and putting it back together: “What we use a lot is chopping and sampling, this kind of collage, things colliding. Sometimes they’re all together, sometimes we really like the contrast.” The same goes for how the four handle it on stage, where the play is in the treatment, not the tunes: “Maybe the songs don’t seem that playful, but how we manage our material is super playful. Viia is playing with four mallets [on the percussion], I’m on the synth and then the guitar. It’s collage in that sense.“ The same collage habit carries into the lyrics, starting with language. Sometimes the four sing three languages at the same time, like a group chanting together, each in their own language instead of settling on a shared one. For Tukre, that’s the point: “We don’t make these language compromises.” The words themselves usually start from folk songs and folk tales, which she reworks before they can be sung now: “The language tends to be quite archaic and doesn’t always fit with the world we live in. So we like to shape it a little and add some reference points we can relate to, but keep the original idea our ancestors had in their folk songs.” The shaping mostly falls to her, in Spampinato’s words “the poet of the band“. A song’s meaning is often sketched in English first, but the language it ends up in is chosen by ear, and for Moore sound decides it: “We’re a lot based on the sound, so what sound are we searching for? That’s where the language plays a big role.” Syllable counts settle much of it: “Some songs require Estonian lyrics, you can just feel it fits better, and some songs are Latvian. The number of syllables each language uses for one word can be different, so we use that to our advantage. How many syllables do we need? And just the pure phonetics of it.” “pa saulei”, the single they released in June, is written and sung in Latvian and takes the idea down to a single word. Saule is sun, pasaule is world, and pa saulei means following the sun. Moore sums up the trick: “If you add these little syllables before and after it, it can change the meaning.“ Like everything they put out, the song never leaves the band’s hands. The four handle the engineering, mixing and visuals themselves, and for Spampinato that’s the most independent way to work: “We do everything by ourselves: recording, mixing, and even some of the visuals. It’s holistic, even though I don’t like the word. It’s maybe the most independent thing you can do, just do everything.” The setting shifts every time. Their debut was made outdoors in Ērgļi, a village in Latvia, with the instruments caught as part of the surrounding soundscape. The follow-up, due in April 2027, moves indoors to Moore’s house and home studio: “We think we need that kind of closeness, but still the comfort.” The shift is deliberate: “I don’t know what the next album will be, probably in a spaceship. But every time we try to come up not only with new music, but with a new way of approaching it.“ That album will carry the material they played at Viljandi Folk, and the second single from it comes first. “meneki tükk” comes out of exactly that care about origins, and the four of them trace it back to a herding call: “It’s the song of going, an arrangement of a horn melody traditionally played when calling a herd to the next pasture for finding food.” The source is a 1912 recording in the Estonian Folklore Archives, a buckhorn player named Jukk Akkermann from Karula, in south-eastern Estonia. The band built the track around his horn, the old recording running against everything they play on top of it: “Jukk’s horn is sounding throughout the piece together with crashing drums, detuned kokles, while the violin brings the old ancient melody as a light torch, dragging along rough horns into its timbre.” The single arrives in late September, with the Baltic daylight already shrinking by a few minutes a day: “we’re stepping into the darker side of the year with this one. It’s our ritual song for finding a way through, and trusting the road even when light is only a horn.” Those darker months will also take them on the road, with Helsinki confirmed for 20 November as part of the Global Club Nights series, then release concerts in April in Latvia, Estonia and, they hope, Helsinki again. For anyone hearing them for the first time, the band’s own introduction says it best: “Tell Your Birds is a four-person music collective of musicians from Latvia, Estonia and Italy. We play our original compositions with collages of Estonian, Latvian and Italian traditional folk melodies and archive recordings and texts.“   Tell Your Birds released "Meneki Tükk" today, 9 October, with the album due in April 2027 and everything in between turning up on their Instagram       The post Interview: Tell Your Birds – Writing a Tradition for Later (September 2026) appeared first on Rhythm Passport.

items._cn_summary: Tell Your Birds是一支由四位在赫尔辛基西贝柳斯学院求学的音乐人组成的乐队，成员分别来自爱沙尼亚、拉脱维亚和意大利。他们将波罗的海传统乐器——kokle、hiiu kannel、巴拉风——与现场电子处理结合，以爱沙尼亚语和拉脱维亚语双语演唱，将民间旋律拆解重组后融入原创作品。新专辑在户外森林中录制，乐器与环境声共同纳入录音，延续了早期《Pause in Nature》和《Carry on with Hope》的田野录音美学。作品涉及传统来源的合法性、为尚未发生的时代创作的旋律，以及语言音节对歌曲归属的决定作用。乐队仅在集中创作时相聚数日，之后各自回到赫尔辛基、维尔扬迪和里加，这是其工作方式的典型节奏。文章发表于单曲《Meneki Tükk》发行之际，内容为采访实录而非纯乐评。

items.body: As I already had the privilege to write a feature about the posthumously released album Stellar Regions on this blog, i want to stretch this even a bit further. Here, I take a look at the period to follow, which eventually and fatally turned out to be the last five months in John Coltrane’s life. My focus is on the production of music in this final stage, as far it has been recorded and released, rather than John’s personal or health condition. On 15 February 1967, John had recorded the tracks eventually released as Stellar Regions in 1995 (see my earlier feature) with the quartet. One week later, on 22 February 1967, he returned with Rashied Ali for a saxophone – drums duo session, eventually to be released as Interstellar Space (see Gary Chapin‘s feature on this album). On 07 March 1967, in another session with the quartet again, he recorded two tracks, as far as we know, Ogunde and Number One . Ogunde is, first of all, a relatively short piece at a few seconds over 3 ½ minutes. A noticeable parallel to Stellar Regions , where the title track and Iris have approximately the same length and concise structure. The track takes its title presumably from an afro-brazilean folk song „Ogundu Varere“, rougly translated as a prayer to the gods. John occupied himself with spiritual traditions especially from Africa. John uses his forceful, cry-like late saxophone sound, overblowing his instrument, which gives an emotional urgence to the piece. The theme starts with a solemn, hmyn-like melody, but breaks out in free, atonal outbursts, before it fades away. In summary, John condenses the intensity of his (at that time) usually half-hour long live improvisations into less than a handful of minutes (but see below, what happened live). At some time in spring (David S. Wild confirmed in the liner notes for Stellar Regions that this track was not recorded on 15 February, so the actual recording date remains unknown), John must have recorded To Be , where he plays flute and is rejoined by Pharoah Sanders on piccolo flute. He shows a very calm, introspective and meditative side here. At over 16 minutes playing time, this track feels like a spiritual retreat. The two flutes give it an airy, almost floating mood. Alice Coltrane’s flowing piano style provides a mystic, harp-like cushion. Rashied Ali on drums and Jimmy Garrison on bass keep it calm and subdued. All together, the piece lacks a trditional jazz pulse, even leaves traditional jazz structures completely and makes a profound structural switch towards a meditative, open-end spiritual incantation. It stands as one of the most explicit artifacts of the creative partnership between John and Alice at that final stage and already mirrors the „cosmic jazz“ landscapes that Alice would pioneer on her own in the years to follow in her landmark solo releases ( Universal Consciousness , Journey in Satchidananda). Not to forget about Pharoah Sanders (Karma). Also unknown is the exact recording date for the piece titled Expression in spring 1967 with the quartet, which later lended its title to the album. 23 April 1967 is the date of the last live recording, The Olatunji Concert. This performance, originally recorded for a radio broadcast, is featured by Fotis Nikolakopoulos on this blog, so see there. With due respect to Fotis, I will limit myself here to the absolutely striking contrast between the live version of Ogunde and the studio version. Performed live, it swells to 28 minutes playing time. The studio recording’s tight and condensed structure is only preserved in the theme at the beginning to which it returns only at the very end. In between, it gets overwhelmed by a storm-like wave of pure energy. After the introduction of the melody as theme, the structure collapses completely in a ritual storm. A dense, polyrhythmic vortex is unchained in Rashied Ali’s drumming. Alice Coltrane plays cascade-like runs on the piano. On saxophone, Pharoah Sanders adds his bone-rattling, ecstatic overblowing cries. Yes, the quartet has been expanded here. Pharoah Sanders is back at it on the second saxophone. Two additional percussionists joined in, Algie DeWitt and Jumma Santos. The last ever live gig came at Baltimore’s Famous Ballroom on May 7, 1967. No audio recording of that performance is known to exist. On 17 May 1967, exactly two months before John’s death, a sextet met for a last studio recording. The master tapes have been lost or at least unissued so two tracks with the titles None Other and Kaleidoscope have been unreleased so far and do not even appear on retrospective compilations. With the recorded material, a last studio record was conceived during John’s lifetime. It was given the title Expression . John was actively involved in the production and met with Bob Thiele. On side 1, it had Ogunde as the opening track (the studio version, as above, of course). Track #2 was To Be with John and Pharoah Sanders on flutes (as above). At over 16 minutes, it was the longest track, making up for nearly half of the original album’s playing time, and the only track on the album in which Pharoah Sanders made an appearance. Side 2 opened with the majestic ballad Offering , the only track chosen from the 15 February session, thus making it the only track on the posthumous album Stellar Regions (see there) that had been released before and had an original title. Hank Shteamer has just featured this track prominently in the New York Times and put it into the larger context of spiritual jazz, for which a piece like Offering „would seem like a perfect prototype“ (Hank Shteamer, Spiritual Jazz Has Turned Cozy. John Coltrane Demanded More. New York Times, September 18, 2026). The original album closed with the title track Expression, John‘s last studio recording to ever be released. In the later CD release only, Number O ne, recorded on the same day as Ogunde , was added as a bonus track (the track, however, had been released for the first time in a 1978 compilation album). Obviously, the most recent recording session of May 1967 was not considered in the process at all (at that time, the tapes at least should still have been around, I guess?). John reportedly selected the four tracks for the original album release and their exact sequence himself. On Friday, 14 July 1967, three days before his death, he met Bob Thiele, handed the master tapes over to him and finally authorised the title and the release of the album, but expressed his opposition against liner notes. Expression , as John Coltrane’s final statement, was released in September 1967, two months after his death, containing John‘s chronologically last audible studio recordings and being the first posthumous release of his music. items.body: “Sound is a haunting, a ghost, a presence whose location in space is ambiguous and whose existence in time is fleeting. The intangibility of sound is uncanny – a phenomenal presence both in the head, at its point of source and all around, and never entirely distinct from auditory hallucinations. The close listener is like a medium who draws out substance from that which is not entirely there.” – David Toop, Sinister Resonance Vanitas came about in the winter of 2018. At the time, Marcus Fischer and Burke Jam were involved in a collaborative performance for the Portland ambient series Bloom, and its title, taken from the 17th-century painting tradition which points to the inevitability of change, the transience of vanity, and the ephemerality of human life, fits in well with the fragile morphing of its music. Nothing stays the same forever; nothing remains in one place. Some are allergic to it, averting their eyes from the prospect or avoiding it entirely, but it will always happen. Resistance is futile. The two musicians share musical and geographic similarities. Fischer’s music draws upon inclement weather patterns, so much a mainstay of Portland, Oregon and a regular feature on The Weather Channel, summoning rain while concentrating on memory and the manipulation of physical audio recording mediums for more of a genuine sound. The locale breathes through into the music. No matter where one may be, no matter the distance, it’s possible to take a vacation. The only baggage is a pair of headphones. Working with the delicate and organic nature of tape, the drones give off a warm, balanced, and temperate atmosphere which is still susceptible to change, darkening skies, and the flickering of falling rain; Fischer’s music is music of subtlety and deep listening. As a composer, artist, curator and educator, Jam explores sound as a means of intervention – ‘questioning and subverting perceptual coherence and relationships with physical place’. He received a Fulbright Grant to Iceland, where he researched environmental sound and methods of listening. Drawing inspiration from the environment (not through any superficial or airy ideas but from active study), Jam’s field recordings and careful, distilled compositional techniques are a form of deep research, actively pursuing acoustic ecology while engaging the listener in the Anthropocene and its effects on sound and surrounding. A record of meticulous detail would be expected, but it’s not so much about detail as it is the musical content and what it’s capable of. Thankfully, underneath the science, the two collaborators create a rewarding and gentle ecosystem of warm minimalism, finding a pocket of air in which to breed, intelligently executed and deep in its considerations. As is true with dying stars and their interstellar clouds of gas, birth, death, and change are universal realities. Galaxies aren’t immune, either. Closer to home, it’s seen in the changing of the seasons and the opening of nature’s new roots. The evolving drones are quiet and subdued shape-shifters. Slightly exotic and warmer tones come to greet the listener amicably, but nothing feels forced. Instead, the soft hues change colour as the music changes temperature, oscillating between small, almost-imperceptible degrees and tiny differences in current and flow. www.dragonseyerecordings.bandcamp.com

items.body: All sounds occur within a space, and changing the properties of that space can be a useful way of creating new and interesting sounds. Designing spaces in order to achieve certain acoustic effects dates back at least as far as ancient Greek amphitheatres, a history that also encompasses medieval churches and cathedrals, Victorian lecture theatres, and modern concert halls. On their tour of resonant spaces in the Czech Republic in 2015, the trio of George Cremaschi, Irene Kepl, and Petr Vrba performed and recorded in a small church, two monasteries, and a hall in the former summer palace of a royal family, always seeking out architectures that provided the right balance of reverberation and airiness. “Resonators” presents some of the results of their efforts. ‘Affective Labor’ begins with deep double bass notes and tentative resonant tones, maintaining a slow, tense pace. There’s a weightlessness to this music, as if the quivering violin, distorted growls, and buzzing tones were floating in zero gravity — an effect undoubtedly related to the reverberation times of the space it is sounding in, the lengths of these times giving an impression of the scale of the architecture. Later, a thick, raspy squeal from Vrba’s trumpet leads into a big crescendo that suddenly drops back down to near-silence again. A similar sense of weightlessness also pervades ‘Locus Resonatus’, but here multiple looped tones are layered on top of each other to create gorgeous, shifting harmonies. Eventually the chords and resonances combine to fill a broad audible spectrum, a field of sound without any single anchor point, before a loud bright trumpet tone provides a locus around which the other instruments gather. Two shorter, spikier pieces from Kepl complete the album, their piercing squeaks, deep thrums, pops, buzzes, and thumps using the resonance of the space in which they sound to emphasise attack and suddenness. This trio are far from the first experimental musicians to recruit the resonance of spaces in order to achieve interesting acoustic effects, but they do so extremely well: “Resonators” is full of surprises, complexity, beauty, and nuance, offering music full of real depth and tension while remaining open to the transformations wrought by resonance and reverberations. George Cremaschi Irene Kepl Petr Vrba Another Timbre Image by Matthias Halibrand

items.body: THIEF, the Los Angeles-based dark electronic project of multi-instrumentalist Dylan Neal, released the single and video “Poison Drum” on October 8. The track follows lead single “Moon and Kill” and is taken from Neal’s new album “Sermons from the Pit,” due November 27 on Prophecy Productions. “Poison Drum” is available to stream on all digital platforms. “Sermons from the Pit” will be released as a 48-page two-CD hardcover artbook with bonus tracks, as a limited gatefold splatter bone-colored vinyl LP pressed to 250 copies, and as a black vinyl LP. Dylan Neal on the ‘cathedral clipping’ technique behind ‘Poison Drum’ Neal describes “Poison Drum” as “the ninth stratum of the pit,” drawing on the Sanskrit concept of nirveda, a term for detachment and disillusionment with worldly pursuits. He said: “Its voice is that of a prophet and its technique is a snare. […] Can you hear the sound of the poison drum? This track prominently features a technique used throughout the album that I call ‘cathedral clipping’, where a sound – in this case a synth – is pushed first through a short convolution reverb and then completely obliterated in gain and re-amping.” Neal recorded and mixed “Sermons from the Pit” himself. Mastering was handled by John Greenham, whose credits include Death Grips and Billie Eilish. The album’s eleven tracks are “Violent Bloom,” “Moon and Kill,” “Axe Swung Ritual,” “Mirror Mirror,” “Sun Slasher,” “Year of the Leech,” “Sermons from the Pit,” “Comet Sorcery,” “Poison Drum,” “Anaphora” and “Closing Scene.” THIEF announces West Coast tour dates THIEF will tour the West Coast in support of “Sermons from the Pit,” opening January 14 in Vancouver. Tickets go on sale October 14. Confirmed dates: January 14 – Vancouver, BC @ Astoria January 15 – Seattle, WA @ Mountain Room January 16 – Portland, OR @ Azoth January 17 – Eugene, OR @ John Henry’s January 20 – Sacramento, CA @ Cafe Colonial January 22 – Santa Cruz, CA @ Crepe Place January 23 – Atascadero, CA @ No Quarter About THIEF THIEF is the solo studio project of Los Angeles-based multi-instrumentalist Dylan Neal, who was formerly the hammered dulcimer player in San Francisco experimental black metal band BOTANIST. Neal launched THIEF with “Thieves Hymn in D Minor” in 2016, followed by “Map of Lost Keys” in 2019 and “The 16 Deaths of My Master” in 2021. The same year, THIEF and BOTANIST released the split album “Cicatrix/Diamond Brush.” Neal has described THIEF’s sound as “Dungeon Pop,” a fusion of trip-hop atmosphere, jungle and drum’n’bass rhythms, industrial textures, glitched choral samples and extreme distortion, built around a signature production approach he calls “cathedral clipping.” The project has been featured by Decibel and NOISEY, and its influences range from Portishead and Ulver to Tool and Nine Inch Nails. THIEF’s 2024 album “Bleed, Memory” was a deeply personal record; “Sermons from the Pit” turns that introspection toward anger, grief, disillusionment, violence and spiritual questioning, arriving at what Neal describes as the possibility of empathy and release. While THIEF remains a solo studio project, Neal performs the material live with a full band, and will bring “Sermons from the Pit” to the West Coast in January.

items.body: Porque no vienes a buscarme? Por qué me ignoran así? Me niegan el sol y el mar… Over the course of their nearly 20-year long tenure, Argentinian (by way of Berlin) post-punk project Mueran Humanos has remained one of our absolute favorite modern bands. Their command of melody, knack for experimentation, captivating dual vocal attack, and passionate live performances put them in a class all their own, and the duo’s four albums and numerous singles remain in heavy rotation to date. Unfortunately, all good things come to an end, as the duo split in February of last year. We’ve been champing at the bit since then, waiting to see what, if anything would come next, and with that in mind, we’re honored to premiere the lead single from Carmen Burguess, titled “El Mar.” Similar to Burguess’ previous work, “El Mar” is a perfect blend of catchy melodies, deep grooves, seductive vocals, and bouncy synths. While the track seems playful at first glance, “El Mar” takes a deliciously moody turn at the halfway point, with a perfectly maneuvered key change giving way to distorted minor synth chords, adding a welcome bit of mystery to an otherwise dance floor-ripe single. As always, Burguess keeps you listeners on their toes, a common and welcome thread throughout her work over the years. Fans of Chris & Cosey, HTRK, Harry, and romantic new wave songstresses such as Nico, Laurie Anderson, and Marianne Faithfull will find much to love in the track, which continues to open up like a fine wine after several listens. Check out to “El Mar” below: El Mar by Carmen Burguess While Burguess has remained active in other mediums over the last few years, “El Mar” is the first taste of new recorded music from Burguess since the final Mueran Humanos LP, which Burguess sang in entirety. Her upcoming solo LP, Flores de Cuero, will be released digitally on January 15th, 2027 via Mixta Music, with a vinyl edition to follow later in the year. The LP was written and recorded between her hometown of Buenos Aires, Argentina, and Berlin. Following the release of the LP, Burguess will perform live in Buenos Aires, Mexico City, and Berlin. Burguess has also just launched her own website, which serves as a living archive for her multimedia work: stories, dream journals and drawings will be released over time, beginning with an unpublished short story, written entirely in Spanish, which is released in tandem with “El Mar.” Stay tuned over there for more of the Flores de Cuero story as it unfolds… Follow Carmen Burguess: Pre-save Flores de Cuero Bandcamp Website Instagram Linktree   The post Multimedia Artist and Synth Chanteuse Carmen Burguess Returns with Alluring Single “El Mar” appeared first on Post-Punk.com.

items.body: “It is about hiding nothing” German grammar gives death a masculine identity, an administrative decision Die Tödin has taken the liberty of correcting. With an arresting voice, a fine ear for melody, and a sharp sense of the absurd, she has become one of darkwave’s most distinctive personalities. A microphone, a MIDI controller, and Ableton provide the tools; she supplies the morbid wit and conviction. There is an elegance to that economy, particularly in the way she makes the bleakest observation sound like a perfectly reasonable complaint. Her dark electronic beats keep the flesh moving, even when the lyrics have reservations about the whole business of being alive. Die Tödin initially took shape in the West German city of Gelsenkirchen, where industrial surroundings, limited prospects, and the useful luxury of being left alone provided room to work. Although she has recently moved away from that bleak environment, her songs retain the resolve of someone carving out her own space when society has failed to offer any. Musically, the basslines and beats come first, followed by the words and vocals. Likewise, German and English share the microphone, sometimes for comic effect and sometimes to establish distance. That instinct extends across yet another language in the Spanish refrain of La Bruja / Die Geister, die ich rief. Even the designation “trve darkwave” borrows black metal’s spelling habits with a straight face, and whether anyone catches the joke is someone else’s problem. Her wit is matched by equally formidable candor. For instance, her song “Angepasste Spießerschweine” takes aim at status-conscious conformity, while “Dissonanz des Lebens” speaks openly about mental illness and the pressure to keep it hidden. Meanwhile, “Die Tödin” distinguishes the project’s focus on lyrics and performance from the immediate emotional expression of her other work as Strobo.Lolita. Although both draw on deeply personal psychological states, she gives each experience a clear musical identity. Just as impressive is the self-possession with which she protects that identity when choosing collaborators. Her forthcoming self-titled collection brings nine recordings from 2022–2025 to Heartworm Press, the label founded by Cold Cave’s Wesley Eisold. Due October 30, 2026, Die Tödin expands upon the earlier Selected Singles release on Minimalkombinat. She regards the collection as a way to bring closure to a difficult period in her life, and the recordings remain unchanged for this edition. We spoke with Die Tödin about the mysterious woman behind the name, the usefulness of being left alone, her relationship with Heartworm Press, and the pleasure of leaving an audience uncertain whether she is joking. Listen to Angepasste Spießerschweine below, then read our conversation with Die Tödin. Your very first song as Die Tödin, “Ich bin schon tot,” name-checks Einstürzende Neubauten, Throbbing Gristle, Peter Murphy, Nosferatu, and Dracula. Which records, books, and films first gave Die Tödin her identity, and which of your formative influences would surprise listeners? There aren’t really any surprises. Die Tödin’s identity didn’t evolve so much through the influence of records, books, and films, rather, it is rooted in a personal history of mental suffering. Themes like suicidality and depression have played a major role in shaping the persona. But to name someone anyway, I really adore artists like Beta Evers. Also, the track “Frustration” by Soft Cell from the Mutant Moments EP was kind of an influence on Die Tödin. You have also worked as Strobo Lolita, drawing more directly from industrial music, no wave, noise, and performance art. What required Die Tödin to become a separate project, and do techniques or ideas ever pass between those two identities? Strobo.Lolita prioritizes raw, immediate emotions, whereas Die Tödin focuses on lyrical content and performance. The only thing the two projects actually have in common is that they represent profound expressions of a psychological state. You describe the city you are from, Gelsenkirchen, through its lack of prospects, industrial nature, cemeteries, physical roughness, and sense of chosen isolation. Can you tell us more about your experience there, and if we can hear the city within the music itself, whether in the rhythms, synthesizer tones, repetition, lyrics, or empty space? You can definitely hear that in the lyrics! Gelsenkirchen is anti-social, and so is Die Tödin. What I liked most about the place was that people left me alone and I had my own space to make music. There are so many poor and unemployed people there, too. So no one noticed that I was in a similar situation, and it didn’t matter that I was just another person who didn’t fit into society. By the way, I moved away recently, so no more Gelsenkirchen. German ordinarily gives death a masculine form, der Tod, while Die Tödin turns that figure female. Why was that particular name important, and what can Die Tödin express that you might be unable or unwilling to express under your own name? As I mentioned before, Die Tödin deals with suicide, death, and transience. Therefore, it makes the most sense to choose a name that embodies these themes. And since I am a woman and express my innermost self through music, Die Tödin had to be female as well. “Trve Darkwave from Gelsenkirchen” began partly as a joke about “trve Norwegian black metal,” although you have also connected it to genuine pessimism and misanthropy. As the project reaches listeners outside the German underground, are you concerned that some of its self-irony may be lost in translation? Sure, but I don’t think that’s a problem. The music itself can create enough atmosphere to carry the emotions, even if people don’t understand the lyrics. That’s exactly the beauty of music. By the way, even Germans sometimes don’t catch the irony. They find themselves asking, “Is she serious?” How did your relationship with Heartworm Press begin? Who approached whom, which recording first caught the label’s attention, and what convinced you that Heartworm understood Die Tödin? Wes reached out to me completely out of the blue, and it didn’t take long until I was convinced that Heartworm Press and Die Tödin were a perfect match. They act in my best interests as a musician, are artists themselves, and I really like the work they have published. I don’t know which song caught their attention first, but the first one they asked me about was “Ich bin schon tot.” We also didn’t know whether it was supposed to be just a single or a longer release. Heartworm Press was founded by Cold Cave’s Wesley Eisold to release his own recordings and writing before expanding into an international home for singular underground voices. Why does it feel like the right label for Die Tödin, and what do you hope the partnership will make possible without compromising the project’s independence? I have a very specific vision for what I create as Die Tödin, and I am very selective when it comes to collaborations. They worked closely with me, and it was important to them that everything was done in my best interest. They made me feel that they wanted to support me and truly valued the fact that I was working with them – and not the other way around. The self-titled Heartworm Press release gathers nine recordings made between 2022 and 2025. Why did this particular moment call for a definitive collection, and why was Die Tödin the right title rather than something that identified it as an anthology or retrospective? The last two years have been very difficult for me, so I want to draw a symbolic line under that period with this release. It isn’t an album, but rather almost everything Die Tödin has released to date. For me, this collection marks the conclusion of this chapter. The original release on Minimalkombinat was titled Selected Singles, now a few more tracks have been added, and a self-titled release seemed the obvious choice for the international market. How did you determine the sequence and final selection? Was there a reason the nine-minute “Nacht” remained outside the collection, and were any of the chosen tracks remastered, remixed, or otherwise altered for this edition? The two songs that didn’t make it onto the record have no recognisable lyrics and aren’t played live. Consequently, they have something of a hidden track quality and aren’t quite typically tödish. The other songs remained unchanged. Earlier editions became extraordinary physical objects, including a one-sided clear record with screen-printed henbane artwork and a special version involving black candles, roses, and petals pressed into the vinyl. The Heartworm pressing comes on Black Static or White vinyl with an 11-by-17-inch newsprint poster. How closely were you involved in shaping this edition, and what role does your continuing visual collaboration with Schwarze.Leere play in the identity of Die Tödin? Schwarze.leere is closely connected with Die Tödin and understands the visual aesthetic. The extras for the special editions were primarily ideas from Minimalkombinat. For the current release, after we had discussed the visual concept together, Amy from Heartworm Press showed me her designs, and I was immediately on board. Listen to Selected Singles below: Selected Singles by Die Tödin “Angepasste Spießerschweine” attacks a mindset governed by status, consumption, narrowness, and hostility toward alternative lives, including versions of that behavior found inside subcultures. As darkwave becomes increasingly fashionable and commercially visible, where do you currently see conformity reproducing itself within the scene? I don’t really keep up with the scene anymore and prefer to spend my time on my own. That’s why I can’t give you an answer to that. You have previously stated that your songs generally begin with a bassline and beat, with the words and vocals arriving last, and that the first vocal take is often the strongest. Which song departed most radically from that method, and how has your minimal setup of Ableton, microphone, and MIDI controller changed since the earliest recordings? To be honest, work on every song begins exactly like that, and the setup hasn’t really changed either. Your lyrics move freely between German and English, while “La Bruja / Die Geister, die ich rief” introduces a Spanish refrain. Do different languages create different degrees of intimacy, distance, humor, or severity, or are those choices guided primarily by rhythm and the physical sound of the words? Yes, it has to do with humor and a sense of detachment. Most of it happens intuitively. In German, many neologisms, especially from English, are already in use, so it felt quite natural. The songs approach despair through very different forms: “Gift” (an interesting word with a double meaning in translation) places poisonous plants beside a ruined fairy tale, “Wild” turns catastrophe into dance music, “Verderben” reduces existence to repetition and vacancy, and “La Bruja” finds companionship among ghosts. How has your lyrical voice developed across those recordings, and what connects these different approaches in your mind? I think it is still far too early in the story of Die Tödin to speak of anything having developed. Listen to Verderben below: Verderben by Die Tödin “Dissonanz des Lebens” directly names psychiatric medication, therapy waiting lists, exhaustion, self-harm, and suicidal ideation. How do you decide what can be disclosed in a song and what must remain private? Has the response from listeners changed how you think about presenting these subjects without diminishing their severity? It is about hiding nothing. In their daily lives, people with mental illness already have to hide so much. On stage, Die Tödin has to let everything out unfiltered, because it is the only way to endure that state of being. People with mental illness are increasingly being pushed into a corner and left to fend for themselves. There are cutbacks everywhere, and help is no longer available. It is important to address this and deal with it openly. As for the people who think this is sick or inappropriate – they haven’t understood the meaning of the lyrics, and Die Tödin simply isn’t the right artist for them. Onstage, you use instrumental playback to give yourself complete freedom of voice and movement, surrounding the performance with corpsepaint, candles, incense, altars, and other carefully chosen elements. With the Heartworm release bringing Die Tödin to a larger international audience, how do you imagine the project developing from here through new music, expanded performances, or shows beyond Europe? I don’t overthink it, nor do I make it my main focus. Making music is definitely the priority. Ultimately, however, Die Tödin should be present wherever she is needed. Nevertheless, music is what I live for. So it would be great to bring tödish music to the whole world.§ Die Tödin has a knack for keeping interviews honest: a question may arrive dressed in their funeral best and leave with an answer that fits on a postage stamp. Her clarity is part of the appeal. She knows what her work needs, holds the terms of collaboration firmly in her own hands, and gives difficult experiences both musical precision and room to be spoken aloud. These nine recordings from her forthcoming self-titled release offer a fitting introduction to an artist whose melodic instinct is matched by the conviction behind it. She says Die Tödin should be present wherever she is needed. And for anyone tired of being told to put on a happy face, this Lady of Death makes surprisingly good company, especially in that she makes darkwave worth living for. Die Tödin is due October 30, 2026, via Heartworm Press. The first pressing is offered on White vinyl and Black Static vinyl, with the latter limited to 200 copies. Both editions include an 11-by-17-inch newsprint poster. Preorder through Heartworm Press here, or visit the collection’s Bandcamp page. items.body: Nick Viola Soft Brutalism Valley Electroniks Soft Brutalism is an apt title for the last EP of industrialized techno from Los Angeles’ Nick Viola. Like much of his work as a producer, the sound is informed by the cacophony of rhythmic noise, but shaped into intriguing an hypnotic shapes through subtle variation. The title track sets the tone quickly, pounding out distorted kicks and percussion sounds, quickly introducing a delayed synthline whose subtle modulation and filter moves cause it to snake and slide between each massive drum hit. “Atrial” varies the approach by omitting almost all melodic aspects of the track, putting textured synths deep into the background of the track behind it’s kick and cymbals, the occasional vocal sample adding to the song’s organic cadence, which evokes breathing at panic attack pace. “Debiasing” fascinates by keeping its rumbling drums deep down in the mix, almost subconscious in comparison to the clacky percussion and sweeps of degraded noise and static that float through the mix. While the remixes from Spheric and FTSM take distinctly different tacks, there’s still a sense of Viola’s own astute compositional approach present, one that finds small moments and soft touches even amongst the most caustic surroundings. Soft Brutalism by Nick Viola Plague Clock Acid Rain self-released The latest in a series of EPs from California producer Plague Clock, Acid Rain, crams an idiosyncratic and unassuming mix of noise, synthpunk, and unreconstructed industrial into a fifteen minute run time. The album title’s well chosen, as you’re getting bright squalls of feedback and pinched, wormy programming which eschew subtlety or compositional ambiance for the sake of direct, squelchy excess collapsing on top of itself. Loops and grooves falling in and out of phase with one another are the driving force here, with the emergent rhythms of “Acid Homunculus” and “Cursed Space Elevator” suggesting an odd middle ground between Skullflower and the BBC Radiophonic Workshop. Elsewhere, the bright spacetrucking of “Void Miasma” and techno blizzard of “Don’t Breathe This” point to a host of electronic influences well outside of the dark “scene” histories which often accompany any industrial released after the mid 80s. Approachable and direct, there’s a lot of texture here for your time. Acid Rain by Plague Clock The post Observer: Nick Viola & Plague Clock appeared first on I Die: You Die.

items.body: “Na Dem Dey Enjoy Pass” comes straight out of everyday Nigerian conversation, Pidgin for “They are the ones enjoying the most.” Said out loud, it asks who gets to enjoy the good life and who is left out of it. “Dem” means “them”, and Lagos Thugs left it undefined on their new single, so every listener decides who they are. Blaring live horns and driving percussion carry the song, with vocals pitched for singing along and a groove for dancing. Singer, saxophonist and multi-instrumentalist Adetunji Adeyemi formed the group in Lagos in 2020 and leads its twelve musicians today. He started it to carry on what Fela Kuti began with Africa 70 and Egypt 80. Fela pioneered afrobeat in the early 1970s, and its politics brought him into violent conflict with Nigeria’s military governments. The grooves follow classic afrobeat, with a heavy bass line and patterns that loop over and over. The percussion draws on Cuban and West African drumming, and jazz and dub find their way in. Their first gig was at Bature Brewery in Lagos in January 2021. Rhythm Passport’s own Lucas Keen caught up with them the following month for the Rendez-Vous à Bobo podcast, when the band numbered fifteen and the conversation covered protest and what’s in a name. The debut that followed, Chaos, is four long compositions that run past 35 minutes, and DJ Ness Afro co-produced it with the band for an analogue, warm 1970s sound. Mixto Records, the Los Angeles label behind the new single, has now released it as a vinyl LP. The single and the vinyl arrive as the band takes the full twelve-piece live show beyond Nigeria. The European tour runs from 2 October in Bremerhaven to 25 October in Beskidy, Poland, taking in Germany, Italy, Austria, France and Denmark on the way. items.body: ““Ain’t nobody coming?” [Ali] said to Coltrane. “No, it’s just you and me.” “What are we playing? Is it fast? Is it slow?” “Whatever you want it to be. Come on. I’m going to ring some bells.”” -Quoted by Ben Ratliff in Coltrane: The Story of a Sound . John Coltrane’s sax-drums duo album with Rashied Ali, Interstellar Space , stands as a singular achievement in the history of free jazz. The duo’s restlessness, their commitment to musical exploration and the profound communication taking place between them would create a template that has animated the practice of free jazz to this day. Stef Gijssels, in his 2007 post on this website, wrote the following about that combination of instruments: “[It] offers a total freedom of interaction, but it's like poetry without rhyme, there is no comfort zone to fall back into, no safe haven, no safety net, it's swim or drown.” I think any jazz musicians wanting to tackle the drums/sax duo format must be very brave indeed, knowing that a comparison to Interstellar Space is almost inevitable. But they would also realize the freedom of unfettered expression that comes with it. And great musicians would view that as an opportunity to create something new, to engage in a genuinely novel musical conversation. Best of all, we get to eavesdrop on that conversation. I’ll always click on a drum/sax duo when I come across one on bandcamp. But I was especially happy to see this particular combo as I was familiar with both musicians and had very much appreciated earlier work of theirs. Both were in a trio album with Tim Berne, Poiēsis , one of the best albums of 2025. Drummer, percussionist Nava Dunkelman was also in a tremendous duo with violinist gabby fluke-mogul, titled Likht. Saxophonist Masayo Koketsu has a solo album, entirely on alto, called Ballade in which she plays jazz standards. She even covers Lover Man . (Seriously, I discovered this album in the course of writing this review and it’s exceptional. Do check it out.) The first track here, 初雷–hatsurai, begins with a thunderburst from Koketsu. Dunkelman matches her intensity. Google Translate tells me the title means First Thunder . Yup. I’ve listened to this album a bunch of times now and it still snaps my head back. These musicians are serious and they want your attention. Both musicians genuinely bring thunder on this track. There’s so much good music on this album, and what’s most impressive is the great variety of ideas to be found. The third track, 露の玉–tsuyu no tama, meaning Dewdrop Ball , is beautiful. Koketsu begins with lightning quick shards of notes with Dunkelman responding with bells. A reference to Interstellar Space ? Then there’s a brief bit of Ayler and then the musicians are off to explore more new ideas. The final and longest track 夕霧–yūgiri, meaning Evening Mist, is the best. It begins with plaintive playing from the saxophone with very light percussion. Then Koketsu’s playing gains in intensity and her lines become more complex. Dunkelman happily matches her and then takes over. Now she’s bringing the thunder and Koketsu again responds. Here, and throughout the album, these two musicians seem so in tune it’s a delight to listen to. Possibly the most surprising thing about this album is the first sentence of the liner notes: “Masayo Koketsu and Nava Dunkelman met for the first time in this studio session.” Veins of Rain by Masayo Koketsu, Nava Dunkelman Email This BlogThis! items.body: Label: ECM Records, 2026 Personnel - Enrico Rava: trumpet; Joe Lovano: tenor saxophone, tarogato; Matteo Paggi: trombone; Francesco Diodati: guitar; Francesco Ponticelli: bass; Evita Pollidoro: drums, vocals. Illustrious Italian trumpeter and composer Enrico Rava, a longtime force on the European jazz scene, returns with his Fearless Five ensemble, welcoming guest saxophonist Joe Lovano, a powerhouse improviser who had collaborated with the bandleader on the live recording Roma (ECM, 2019). All members of the quintet contribute compositions, trusting the bandleader's candidly investigative approach that opposes rigid perceptions. Rava's " Certi Angoli Segreti ", an exceptionally beautiful tune first recorded in 1998, gracefully materializes with beautiful color shades. Francesco Diodati's guitar gives it a particular touch, later soloing with motivic ability and acerbic distortion; Francesco Ponticelli's dynamic bass builds a solid foundation with drummer Evita Polidoro; Lovano's storytelling comes with delightful details; trombonist Matteo Paggi's expressions are grounded and exploratory; and Rava excels in his improvisational fluctuations—sometimes angular and outside, other times hypnotically flowing and distinctively melodic. Rava brings two other previously recorded pieces: " Hitchcock at the Beach ", whose balladic feeling and original beauty are preserved despite emerging here most as a collaborative voice-trumpet meditation; and the exciting " Bowery Dance ", which evokes Rava's New York years with an electrified intro, authoritative bass double-stops, and a crisp backbeat. Lovano and Rava improvise with fire, rejoicing in unison lines in support of their declarations. Lovano is credited with a couple of distinct compositions. The open-ended " Sun Rava " is full of possibilities, incorporating sharp staccato blows, buoyant swing impulses, and clever pedal points, also featuring improvised dialogues between Rava and Paggi, and then Diodati and Lovano, before the saxophonist rambles freely over the bass-and-drums bedrock. " Tone, Shape, and Colours ", a free improvisation based on a riff by Lovano, brings the horn players together in lively conversation. If the rhythm section kicks into high gear on Lovano's pieces, it eases into the softer lyrical flow of Diodati's " Sin Peso ", a burnished ballad suggesting a bolero feel, and Polidoro's " Le Mie Gambe ", which, unfolding in 3/4, features the drummer as a vocalist of surprising intensity. Since the early '70s, Rava—who turned 87 in August—has led a series of highly rewarding albums, and Corners is no exception. items.body: London-based, Australian-born electronic producer, songwriter and DJ HAAi released her third studio album “DIGITiSE” on October 9 via Mute, on vinyl, CD and digitally. The release arrived alongside a video for “Talking Walls,” a collaboration with producer Skybreak and the Colombian children’s choir Cantoalegre. DIGITiSE by HAAi “DIGITiSE” runs to ten tracks: “RE-HUMANiSE” (feat. Kaiden Ford and ILA), “Printerlude,” “Ignition” (feat. Echonomist), “Depth Perception,” “DIGITiSE” (feat. Pat Alvarez), “Technology,” “HUMANiSE Radio,” “THANK U,” “I Wanna Feel Like Someone” (feat. James Massiah) and “HAAi x Skybreak ‘Talking Walls'” (feat. Cantoalegre). The album follows 2025’s “HUMANiSE,” reusing the same closing choir motif on its opening track, and brings in new collaborators Echonomist and Skybreak alongside returning contributors Pat Alvarez, ILA, James Massiah and Kaiden Ford. HAAi described “DIGITiSE” as “HUMANiSE’s” “bigger, ravey sibling,” adding: “DIGITiSE holds the hand of HUMANiSE and walks it to the club.” ‘Talking Walls’ brings in a children’s choir from Medellín HAAi calls “Talking Walls” “one to hug your mates to at the festival.” Cantoalegre, a children’s choir founded in Medellín, Colombia, in 1984, supplies the vocals alongside Skybreak, the production project of New York and London-raised artist Jack Ramsay. HAAi traces the collaboration to a festival booking in Colombia earlier this year: “I’ve had the fortune of playing in Colombia, and more specifically Medellín, many times. It’s a place I hold very dear to my heart. I was there in January to play a festival and felt the urge to reach out about working with a local kids’ choir. Within two hours of having this thought, I was speaking with the principal of Cantoalegre about what I wanted to do. I’ve worked with different choirs across my last two albums, so it was really exciting to be working with new voices in a city I love so much. There was something about hearing the lyrics through the voices of the next generation that gave the words so much more hope and meaning. It’s an experience I will never forget, and I’m so proud of what we made.” On the album as a whole, HAAi said: “I’ve spent so many hours in clubs – on the dance floor and in the booth – and I really wanted to put that into this new album.” Visuals for the campaign are led by Martin Falck, whose past credits include Fever Ray, The Knife and Icona Pop. DJ dates and an Australian tour with The Avalanches HAAi marks the release with an all-night, open-to-close set at EartH in London on October 31, staged with production and set design by Playbody, and a ten-hour marathon set at Refuge in New York on October 18. She has also announced an Australian tour with The Avalanches for March 2027. Confirmed dates: 9 Oct – Geneva (CH), Electron Festival 10 Oct – Manchester (UK), IPC, b2b with DJ Seinfeld, The Warehouse Project 16 Oct – San Francisco, CA (US), Dom Dolla support b2b DJ Seinfeld at Cow Palace 17 Oct – Miami, FL (US), iiiPoints Festival 18 Oct – New York, NY (US), Open to Close, Refuge 22 Oct – Manchester (UK), 20 Years of the Warehouse Project 23 Oct – Amsterdam (NL), b2b Adiel, Audio Obscura x Raw Factory 24 Oct – Galway (IE), Heineken Greenlight 25 Oct – Athens (GR), b2b Romy, Eden 31 Oct – London (UK), HAAi All Night at EartH 20 Nov – Brighton (UK), Concorde 2 21 Nov – Manchester (UK), Depot Mayfield 27 Nov – Los Angeles, CA (US), Time Warp 28 Nov – San Francisco, CA (US), The Great Northern 3 Dec – Miami (US), b2b Salute, Raw Cuts, The Ground 18 Dec – Bristol (UK), b2b Special Request, Mastery x Glade at Prospect 15 Jan 2027 – Johannesburg (ZA), Fabric at Truth Club 16 Jan 2027 – Cape Town (ZA), Castle of Good Hope 19 Feb 2027 – Paris (FR), Polari at FVTVR 5 March 2027 – Melbourne (AU), Royal Botanic Gardens, with The Avalanches 6 March 2027 – Brisbane (AU), On The Banks, with The Avalanches 7 March 2027 – Sydney (AU), Sydney Opera House, with The Avalanches About HAAi HAAi is the stage name of Teneil Throssell, a producer, songwriter and DJ who grew up in Karratha, Western Australia, before moving to the UK to play guitar in the psychedelic rock duo Dark Bells. She began DJing after that band split and held a two-year residency at the London club Phonox from late 2016. Her debut EP, “Systems Up, Windows Down,” came out on Mute on November 14, 2019. The label released her debut album, “Baby, We’re Ascending,” on May 27, 2022, with guests including Jon Hopkins; Pitchfork wrote that the record was “something bigger, something that transcends the club without turning its back on it.” In 2023, HAAi compiled an edition of the “DJ-Kicks” series for !K7 and released “Lights Out,” a collaboration with Fred again.. and Romy. Her second album, “HUMANiSE,” followed on Mute on October 10, 2025, preceded by the singles “Can’t Stand To Lose,” “Shapeshift” (with KAM-BU), “Satellite,” “Hey!” and “Stitches.” The album was named to the year-end lists of Rough Trade, Disco Pogo and Resident, and The Quietus described it as “transcendent.” An accompanying concert film, shot at London’s Drumsheds, featured album collaborators Jon Hopkins, Alexis Taylor, Obi Franky, KAM-BU and TRANS VOICES. “DIGITiSE,” announced in June 2026 and preceded by the singles “Ignition” (feat. Echonomist) and “I Wanna Feel Like Someone” (feat. James Massiah), extends “HUMANiSE’s” themes into a dancefloor-oriented record built from HAAi’s own DJ sets. HAAi was named Beatport’s Artist of the Month over the summer of 2026 and performed a run of shows at London’s Courtyard Theatre and the Royal Albert Hall ahead of the album’s release. “DIGITiSE” is out now on Mute on vinyl, CD and digitally, with HAAi set to tour it through 2026 and into an Australian run with The Avalanches in March 2027.

items.body: Toronto-based producer Andrew Nolan released his new album “Black Dogs” on October 9 through GIVE/TAKE, in collaboration with Justin K Broadrick’s Avalanche Recordings. The ten-track record incorporates industrial dub, hip-hop, drum & bass and downtempo electronic, with contributions from JK FLESH, Metalheadz artist Gremlinz, and Sectra. “Black Dogs” was mastered by Broadrick, who records as JK FLESH and also leads Godflesh and Jesu. Pre-orders opened on October 2 alongside the lead single “The Skriker of Yorkshire,” a collaboration between Nolan and JK FLESH. “Black Dogs” is available now on CD, cassette and digital through GIVE/TAKE and Avalanche Recordings. Black Dogs by Andrew Nolan ‘Black Dogs’ draws on north English folklore The album takes its name from the black dogs of English folklore, spectral hounds said to be the spirits of unbaptized babies. Nolan built its soundscapes from animal sounds, junk metal and feedback, citing Coil, Nurse With Wound, Meat Beat Manifesto, Radiophonic Workshop, Scientist and Depth Charge among his reference points, alongside the golden-era British hip-hop of Hijack, Gunshot and Hardnoise. “The Skriker of Yorkshire” takes its title from a black dog faery hound in English folklore whose shriek announces death. On the collaboration with JK FLESH, Andrew Nolan said: “Despite appearing on multiple records together, Justin and I have only collaborated on one track previously. Much of the direction for ‘Skriker’ came from late night conversations about the UK breakbeat hardcore scene we were both avid followers of in the early 90s. The idea was to use hardware samplers to completely degrade Justin’s material, then rebuild it entirely, keeping the bass intact and chopping overdriven breaks for momentum.” On the album as a whole, Nolan described it as “a reckless invocation of ill omen. All due respects paid to spectral hounds. Man is still the animal.” GIVE/TAKE and Avalanche Recordings have been releasing music together as part of an ongoing collaborative series, of which “Black Dogs” is the latest entry. Nolan marked the release with an online Bandcamp listening party and artist chat on October 9. About Andrew Nolan Andrew Nolan is a Toronto-based producer who has worked in dark ambient, grindcore, industrial noise, hip-hop and death metal for more than three decades. He began in DIY and underground music as a pirate radio DJ in the north of England before relocating to Canada. Nolan has collaborated with Refused, Full of Hell, The Body, Homemade Weapons, Harms Way and Fatboi Sharif, and recently scored the feature film “Hangashore,” starring James Frecheville and Hera Hilmar. In 2019, Nolan began merging tape loop, found sound and synth-collage techniques with the hip-hop production work he was also pursuing. “Black Dogs” pairs industrialized dub with the production approach of golden-era British hip-hop. The album is released on GIVE/TAKE in collaboration with Justin K Broadrick’s Avalanche Recordings and follows a run of recent solo work and collaborative releases that have kept Nolan active across multiple corners of underground electronic and metal music.
